newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to seek more talks between Kurdish factions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to seek more talks between Kurdish factions.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday it would continue to seek a settlement between Iraq's warring Kurdish factions despite the intervention by Baghdad that prompted a U.S. cruise missile strike on Iraq.

"We're not going to give up on our diplomatic effort to try to convince the Kurdish groups to unite more or less out of their own self-interest to oppose the efforts of (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein," a State Department spokesman said.

The State Department said last month it had negotiated a cease-fire between the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and had persuaded them to attend peace talks in London in September.

But the truce quickly collapsed, and Saddam sent troops into the Western-protected Kurdish region in support of the KDP on Friday. The move led the United States to fire 27 cruise missiles at defense installations in southern Iraq on Tuesday.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington would work with the KDP, led by Massoud Barzani, and the Iranian-backed PUK of Jalal Talabani "to try to get them to work together for the benefit of the Kurdish people."
"Our advice to the Kurds is, put aside your differences, which we understand are long-held and quite bitter," Burns told a news briefing.

"Do not accept the offers of either the Iranian leadership or of Saddam Hussein for friendship, because neither of them can be trusted, and neither of them is going to act in the interest of the Kurdish people," Burns said.
Burns said the United States had warned Iran to stay out of the fighting in northern Iraq, "and we reiterate that warning today."

Burns said he could give no specific details of how the United States would pursue its diplomatic effort. "I think we ought to let the dust settle a little bit before that's going to be possible," he said.

Robert Deutsch, head of the State Department's Iran and Iraq section, chaired talks in Ireland last year that led to a temporary truce. Washington has proposed that this time talks be led by Robert Pelletreau, assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs.
